transcript.text: Every so often when I use the hob the electrics in the house go off. Not every time, maybe once a week. It's an induction hob, Hisense I think.

An induction hob tripping the power now and then is fairly common, and it's usually fixable. The main clue is which switch in your consumer unit (fuse box) has flipped when it happens. Next time, check before you reset it.

## What the tripped switch tells you

1. An RCD has tripped (often a wider switch with a "T" test button, and it may cut a whole bank of circuits or the whole house)
This means it detected current leaking to earth. Common causes:
• Moisture in the hob. A spill, boil-over, or wiping it down with a wet cloth can let water reach the electronics underneath. Does it tend to happen after cooking something that bubbles over, or after cleaning?
• A developing fault in the hob. Failing components can leak a little current, enough to trip the RCD sometimes but not always.
• Cumulative leakage. Lots of appliances each leak a tiny, normal amount. If the hob shares an RCD with, say, the washing machine, fridge and kettle, the total can occasionally tip it over. Does it happen when other things are running too?
• Older RCD type. Induction hobs contain electronics that older "Type AC" RCDs can react badly to. Newer installations should use "Type A" or better. The type is usually printed on the device.

2. Only the hob's own circuit breaker (MCB) has tripped (a single narrow switch, usually labelled "cooker" or "hob")
This suggests overload:
• The breaker or cable may be undersized for the hob. Many induction hobs need a 32A circuit, and some installations use less.
• It may happen when you use boost or several zones at full power at once.
• A loose connection at the cooker switch or terminal block can cause heating and tripping.

## What you can try yourself
• Note what's on each time it trips: which zones, boost, other appliances.
• Avoid boil-overs and wipe the hob with a damp cloth, not a wet one, for a week or two to see if it changes.
• Look at the cooker isolator switch on the wall. If it's discoloured, warm, or smells hot, stop using the hob and call an electrician.

## When to get an electrician
Get an electrician if it keeps happening, if you see any scorching, smell burning, or hear buzzing, or if the switch trips again immediately when you reset it. They can test the hob's insulation, check the circuit rating and connections, and tell you whether it's the hob, the wiring, or the RCD. If the hob is still under warranty and the wiring checks out, Hisense should repair or replace it.

If you can tell me which switch trips and roughly what's happening when it does, I can help narrow it down further.

I'm not sure which switch it is, it's a big switch in the middle that drops. It's mostly when two rings are on high, and a couple of times there'd been a boil-over. Once there was a faint electrical smell after it tripped too.

A big switch in the middle that drops is most likely an RCD, which trips when it detects electricity leaking where it shouldn't. Combined with the electrical smell, I'd treat this as a safety issue.

## Stop using the hob until it's checked

A faint electrical smell after tripping suggests something is overheating, either inside the hob or at a connection (the wall isolator switch or the terminal block behind the hob). Under heavy load, like two rings on high, a poor connection or failing component gets hotter and can start leaking current, which fits your pattern. Overheating connections are a fire risk, and the RCD tripping is protecting you, so don't keep resetting it and carrying on.

For now:
• Turn off the hob at its wall isolator switch (the large switch near the cooker, often red or labelled "cooker") and leave it off.
• Check that switch. If it's discoloured, scorched, cracked, or warm when nothing's on, mention it to the electrician.
• If you ever see smoke or scorching, or smell burning that doesn't fade quickly, switch off at the consumer unit and keep away from the hob.

## Get it looked at

Call a registered electrician (in the UK, look for NICEIC or NAPIT registration). Tell them:
• The RCD trips about once a week, mostly with two zones on high
• It has happened after boil-overs
• There was an electrical smell once after a trip

They can test the hob and circuit for leakage, check the connections, and confirm the cable and breaker suit the hob's power rating. If the problem is inside the hob, they'll tell you, and you'd then need a Hisense repair.

Check your warranty. If the hob is less than a couple of years old, a fault like this may be covered, so find your receipt and contact Hisense before paying for a hob repair.

## About the boil-overs

Spilled liquid can seep around the edges or controls and reach the electronics, which would explain some of the trips. That doesn't account for the smell, though, so it's not a reason to skip the check.
